'''''Aria latifolia''''', the '''broad-leaved whitebeam''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''service tree of Fontainebleau''', or '''''alisier de Fontainebleau''''' in French, is a species of [[whitebeam]] that is [[endemism|endemic]] to the area around [[Fontainebleau]], south of [[Paris]] in France, where it has been known since the early eighteenth century.<ref name=rushforth>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref><ref name=afm>Mitchell, A. F. (1974). ''A Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Northern Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-212035-6}}</ref><ref name=afm2>Mitchell, A. F. (1982). ''The Trees of Britain and Northern Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-219037-0}}</ref>

==Description==
''Aria latifolia'' is a deciduous,<ref name = "Jugue, n.d." /> up to 20 m tall tree<ref name = "Beech & Rivers, 2017" /> with a trunk up to 60 cm in diameter.{{cn|date=August 2026}} The bark is smooth and grey, and becomes fissured at the base in old trees.<ref name = "Elwes & Henry, 1906" />{{rp|155}} The [[leaf|leaves]] are 5–10 cm long and broad (rarely, up to 20 cm long and 12 cm broad), but, most typically, the leaves are approximately as broad as they are long. They are green above, downy with greyish-white hairs beneath, with six to ten small triangular teeth along each margin. The [[flower]]s are 1–1.5 cm wide, with five creamy-white petals and yellowish stamens; they are produced in [[corymb]]s about eight centimetres in diameter in mid-spring. The [[fruit]] is a globular, dull brownish-red, [[pome]] of 10–12 mm diameter, dotted with large pale lenticels, ripening in late autumn.<ref name=rushforth/><ref name=afm/><ref name=afm2/> The fruit bears 1–2 seeds.<ref name = "Elwes & Henry, 1906">{{cite wikisource | last1 = Elwes | first1 = Henry John | author1-link = Henry John Elwes | last2 = Henry | first2 = Augustine | author2-link = Augustine Henry | title = The Trees of Great Britain & Ireland, volume 1 | location = Edinburgh | publisher = Privately Printed | date = 1906 | wslink = The Trees of Great Britain & Ireland/Volume 1 | pages = [[:s:en:The Trees of Great Britain & Ireland/Volume 1/Pyrus#155|155–158]]}}</ref>{{rp|155}}
===Cytology===
The chromosome count is 2n = 34.<ref name = "Sell, 1989" />

==Taxonomy==
It was first described as ''Crataegus latifolia'' {{au|Lam.}} by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] in 1779.<ref name = "Lamarck, 1779">Lamarck,  Jean-Baptiste-Pierre-Antoine de Monet de & Gogué & Née (Firm). (1778). Flore françoise, ou, Description succincte de toutes les plantes qui croissent naturellement en France : disposée selon une nouvelle méthode d’analyse, & à laquelle on a joint la citation de leurs vertus les moins équivoques en médecine, & de leur utilité dans les arts (Vol. 3, p. 486). l’Imprimerie Royale. https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/10168136</ref><ref name = "IPNI a">''Crataegus latifolia'' Lam. (n.d.). International Plant Names Index. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://www.ipni.org/n/723664-1</ref> It was moved to the genus ''Aria'' {{au|(Pers.) J.Jacq. ex Host}} as ''Aria latifolia'' {{au|(Lam.) M.Roem.}} by [[Max Joseph Roemer]] in 1847.<ref name = "POWO" />
The tree is of [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] origin, between ''[[Aria torminalis]]'' (wild service tree) and a member of the ''[[Aria edulis]]'' (whitebeam) group, but it exhibits [[apomixis]], breeds true from seed,<ref name=rushforth/> and shows little to no variation.<ref name=edinburgh1882>{{cite journal | author = Ed. | date = 1882-12-09 | title = The Arboretum : ''Pyrus latifolia'' | journal = [[The Gardeners' Chronicle]] | volume = 18 | issue = 467 | page = 749 | url = http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/26084841}} With an illustration.</ref> The ''Aria latifolia'' [[species complex]] includes numerous other species occurring outside of France<ref name = "BIB a">''Sorbus latifolia'' agg. Artengruppe Breitblättrige Mehlbeere. (n.d.). Botanischer Informationsknoten Bayern (BIB). Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://daten.bayernflora.de/de/info_pflanzen.php?taxnr=26801</ref><ref name = "FloraWeb">BfN - Bundesamt für Naturschutz. (n.d.-a). ''Sorbus latifolia'' agg. (Breitblättrige Mehlbeere (Artengruppe)). FloraWeb. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://www.floraweb.de/php/artenhome.php?name-use-id=26801</ref> which are difficult to differentiate<ref name = "Meyer, n.d." /> and other species may frequently be misidentified as ''Aria latifolia''.<ref name = "Sell, 1989">Sell, P. D. (1989). [https://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Wats17p385.pdf The ''Sorbus latifolia'' (Lam.) pers. aggregate in the British Isles.] Watsonia, 17(4), 385-399.</ref> The true ''Aria latifolia'' s. str. is endemic to France.<ref name = "BIB b">''Sorbus latifolia'' (Lam.) Pers. s. str. Breitblättrige Mehlbeere. (n.d.). Botanischer Informationsknoten Bayern (BIB). Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://daten.bayernflora.de/de/info_pflanzen.php?taxnr=6938</ref>

It was at one time thought to be a variety of ''[[Hedlundia intermedia]]'' (Swedish whitebeam), and it was treated as such by some authors, such as [[A. P. de Candolle]] and [[John Claudius Loudon|J. C. Loudon]], during the nineteenth century. Reflecting the considerable difference in opinion over the past two centuries as to its origins and identity, many synonyms have been used for the tree, including ''Crataegus latifolia'' Lam.; ''Pyrus latifolia'' (Lam.) Lindl.; ''P. intermedia'' var. ''latifolia'' (Lam.) D.C., and ''P. edulis'' Willd.<ref name=bean4>Bean, W. J. (1980). ''Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles'' 8th ed., vol. 4. John Murray {{ISBN|0-7195-2428-8}}.</ref>
===Etymology===
The specific epithet ''latifolia'', from the Latin ''latus'' meaning ''broad'', and ''folium'' meaning ''leaf'', means ''broad-leaved''.<ref name = "NZPCN">''Sorbus'' × ''latifolia''. (n.d.). New Zealand Plant Conservation Network. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/sorbus-latifolia/</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Aria latifolia'' [[sensu stricto]] with a restricted distribution around Paris is endemic to France.<ref name = "Beech & Rivers, 2017" /> All of the populations are found within 100 km from the Fountainebleau forest, where it was first discovered.<ref name = "Hensen, 1970">Hensen, K. J. W. (1970). [https://edepot.wur.nl/295401 Het ''Sorbus latifolia''-complex.] Meded. Bot. Tuinen Belmonte Arbor. Wageningen, 13, 181-194.</ref> The introduced population in Britain and Ireland differs from the French population from Fontainebleau.<ref name = "Beech & Rivers, 2017" /><ref name = "BSBI">''Sorbus latifolia'' (Lam.) Pers. (Broad-leaved Whitebeam). (n.d.). Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://bsbi.org/taxa/2cd4p9h.9hm/sorbus-latifolia</ref>

==Conservation==
''Aria latifolia'' is a [[vulnerable species]] with about 1000–8000 individuals growing at 6 locations.<ref name = "Beech & Rivers, 2017" /> It is cultivated in numerous botanic gardens,<ref name = "BGCI PlantSearch">''Sorbus latifolia'' (Lam.) Pers. (n.d.). BGCI PlantSearch. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://plantsearch.bgci.org/taxon/254393</ref> but it is unclear if the plants in these collections represent ''Aria latifolia'' sensu stricto from Fontainebleau, France.<ref name = "Beech & Rivers, 2017" /> The ancient woodlands where it occurs are under the protection of France's ''Office National des Forêts''.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

==Uses==
''Aria latifolia'' is sometimes planted as an ornamental tree in parks, arboreta, botanical gardens, and forests.<ref name = "Meyer, n.d.">Meyer, T. (n.d.). Arten der Artengruppe ''Sorbus latifolia'' agg. Blumen in Schwaben. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://www.blumeninschwaben.de/Zweikeimblaettrige/Rosengewaechse/latifolia_agg.htm</ref> Although it is rare, the edible fruit was sold in markets in Fontainebleau.<ref name = "Jugue, n.d.">Jugue, L. (n.d.). Alisier de Fontainebleau. Reconnaître Les Arbres. Retrieved August 2, 2026, from https://www.reconnaitre-les-arbres.fr/recherche/pages/fiche_plante.php?choix=153</ref> Its homogeneous and long-lasting wood has proved to be valuable for certain uses.{{cn|date=August 2026}}
